# North Meier Outpost

Section: Features

[![North Meier Outpost viewed facing east-south-east, Raptor Lighthouse visible in the top right, St. Alexander Hospital visible in the top left. The green building at the bottom is the harbor workbench, the small building near open space above it is the garage workbench. The sleeping/respawn area is the building at the bottom left.](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/stormworks_gamepedia_en/images/8/8b/North_Meier_Outpost.png/revision/latest/scale-to-width-down/356?cb=20250718133742)](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/stormworks_gamepedia_en/images/8/8b/North_Meier_Outpost.png/revision/latest?cb=20250718133742)

[https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/File:North_Meier_Outpost.png](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/File:North_Meier_Outpost.png)

North Meier Outpost viewed facing east-south-east, Raptor Lighthouse visible in the top right, St. Alexander Hospital visible in the top left. The green building at the bottom is the harbor workbench, the small building near open space above it is the garage workbench. The sleeping/respawn area is the building at the bottom left.

North Meier Outpost is a small outpost in the north-west of the [Arid Island](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Arid_Island), 1.6 km southeast of Raptor Lighthouse and 600m NE of St. Alexander Hospital. It can be purchased for $30,000. There is also an oil deposit with a construction workbench that does not need to be purchased to be used about 2 km SE of the outpost.

For players with the Industrial Frontiers DLC, this is the default starter base for [classic mode](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Gameplay/Gamemodes/Classic).

## Features

It features a small dock and garage. The dock allows for construction of small boats, submarines, and amphibious vehicles up to 14.25x6.75x6.75m. The garage allows for construction of cars, trucks, and small helicopters or VTOLs up to 17.75m (71 blocks) long x 15.75m (63 blocks) wide x 5.25m (21 blocks) tall. A road leads from the garage out to the rest of the island.

Since [V1.6.2](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/V1.6.2), this location and FJ Warner Docks are the only locations guaranteed to spawn a Stormwoof (dog) which can assist the player in locating nearby survivors by barking in their direction.

title: Stormwoof
text:
# Stormwoof

| [![Stub](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/stormworks_gamepedia_en/images/f/f1/Stub_v1.png/revision/latest/scale-to-width-down/64?cb=20250514003444)](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/stormworks_gamepedia_en/images/f/f1/Stub_v1.png/revision/latest?cb=20250514003444) | *This article is a [stub](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Category:Stubs). *You can help Us by [expanding it](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Stormwoof?action=edit). |
| --- | --- |

Stormwoof is the term given to dogs in Stormworks, one of the animals added in the [Industrial Frontier DLC](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Industrial_Frontier_DLC). They can be somewhat helpful in rescue missions by barking in the direction of nearby survivors.

The dog whistle can be used to instruct a Stormwoof to stay (using a long burst), or to come to you (using two short bursts). A Stormwoof placed in a bed or seat will remain there until you move it elsewhere, even if you use two short whistle bursts.

Stormwoofs are guaranteed to spawn at [North Meier Outpost](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/North_Meier_Outpost) and FJ Warner Docks. There are a variety of breeds including the Beagle, Border Collie, Corgi, Daschund, Greyhound, Pug, Shiba, and Vizsla.

title: Damage control
text:
# Damage control

Section: Fire suppression

| [![Stub](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/stormworks_gamepedia_en/images/f/f1/Stub_v1.png/revision/latest/scale-to-width-down/64?cb=20250514003444)](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/stormworks_gamepedia_en/images/f/f1/Stub_v1.png/revision/latest?cb=20250514003444) | *This article is a [stub](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Category:Stubs). *You can help Us by [expanding it](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Damage_control?action=edit). |
| --- | --- |

Vehicles can be damaged in Stormworks in many different ways. In the base game, there is the risk of colliding vehicles with other vehicles or terrain. Additionally, an engine which runs too fast and is inadequately cooled can overheat and catch on fire. Fire can spread to nearby walls and components causing gradually spreading damage. There are also some [missions](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Wiki/Missions) which create substantial risk of vehicle damage, e.g. towing an old sea mine to a port. With the [Search and Destroy DLC](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Search_and_Destroy_DLC), enemy vehicles may also fire guns, rockets, and missiles at player-made vehicles. With the many different ways vehicles can be damaged, it is good practice to prepare vehicles to be able to survive the damage and recover.

## Damage propagation

Damage can spread by fire, by ammunition cookoff, or by warhead detonation.

Damaged batteries and engines can catch on fire. The fire can spread across anything, even normal blocks, unless/until is extinguished. A single uncontrolled fire can eventually destroy an entire ship or aircraft.

Damaged ammo drums which contain ammo can cook off. Several rounds of whatever ammo type they contain will be shot out in random directions around the drum. Large quantities of ammo packed together can easily cause a rapid chain reaction.

Torpedo, missile, and bomb warheads can explode if they are damaged. If they are positioned near each other and one is damaged, it can lead to almost instantaneous detonation of the entire group. EMP warheads will also trigger their EMP effect if damaged.

Rocket launchers, battle cannon belts, artillery cannon belts, and Bertha cannon belts are all safe to damage without risk of chain reaction.

## Bulkheads

Dividing a large ship or submarine into several sections separated by walls along its length and width can help to contain flooding.

### Collision risk

The front of a ship is the area most likely to be damaged in a collision, so the front bulkhead area is generally the most important. To prevent fires it should not contain batteries, ammo, or fuel-driven engines. Additionally, it needs to be sized appropriately. If it's too small, the bulkhead may be damaged along with the hull, leading to further flooding behind it. Thus, it needs to be designed large enough to contain the damage but not overly large so that it remains easy to bilge out if it floods.

## Fire detection

Temperature sensors can detect the added heat of a fire. Once the sensor is broken, it will suddenly report a temperature of exactly 0. A high temperature or 0 temperature can both be taken as signs that an area is likely to have an active fire.

## Fire suppression

At the very least, nearly every vehicle should carry a fire extinguisher. A small upgrade from this for ships likely to have large fires to put out is to include a water pipe running down the length of the vessel supplied by a large pump. With numerous hose attachment points on this pipe, a player can attach a hose to one of the points and use it as a fire extinguisher with unlimited supply.

Where possible, components most likely to catch on fire if damaged, like diesel engines and batteries, should have automatic fire suppression systems. This can be accomplished with fluid cannon nozzles set to a wide spray, or with fluid cannons configured with micro-controllers to automatically spray an area. Temperature sensors can automatically detect that the area is hot (or has been damaged, which would mean probably on fire) and trigger the fluid cannons to douse the fire.

## Repair

[![Fully damaged surface repaired at the red block. Welding torch and mounted welder produce the same result.](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/stormworks_gamepedia_en/images/8/89/Welding_torch_repair.png/revision/latest/scale-to-width-down/180?cb=20250819001905)](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/stormworks_gamepedia_en/images/8/89/Welding_torch_repair.png/revision/latest?cb=20250819001905)

[https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/File:Welding_torch_repair.png](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/File:Welding_torch_repair.png)

Fully damaged surface repaired at the red block. Welding torch and mounted welder produce the same result.

Repair can be done with by hand with welders or underwater welders, or with a vehicle using mounted welders. Most vehicles should have at least a welder and underwater welder for basic manual repairs. Mounted welders use large amounts of electricity but can be run semi-autonomously, e.g. placed on a track and moved down the the length of a ship to weld everything damaged along the hull. They can also reach places that are too small for a player to get into, e.g. a 2x2 tunnel through a ship could fit a compact rail and several welders that weld everything in all directions around the length of the tunnel.

### Lingering effects

Even after being repaired, batteries will still be depleted. Ammo drums that cooked off will be depleted of ammo.

Note that fluid tanks and gas tanks will *not* lose their contents if damaged. Also, warheads that were part of a vehicle/subvehicle which was not too damaged to continue existing can be repaired and detonated again.

## Redundancy

For critical systems, like power, it's generally a good idea to have a redundant backup.

Section: Redundancy > Auxiliary power units (APUs)

## Redundancy

For critical systems, like power, it's generally a good idea to have a redundant backup.

For example, note that a damaged battery will still have zero power after repair. If you needed the battery to start your engine and needed the engine to charge your battery, then you may be left with an inoperable vehicle that you can't get working again. Having a backup battery in a separate location and a circuit breaker to protect it against being drained will allow you to fix your damaged main battery, restart your engine, and then recharge both batteries.

### Manual backups

Hand cranks can be a very useful way to either manually crank an engine to start (if the starter has insufficient power), or to provide initial charge to a battery so basic systems like throttles, buttons, clutches, and starters can be used.

Be aware that clutches do not work without power and they are commonly used to limit power taken by generators. If there's only one battery and one generator and the generator takes power from the engine through a clutch then in the event of battery damage there will be no way to get the vehicle running again unless/until it can be jumpstarted. For this typical situation, it is good practice to have one or two handcranks connected to the generator *after* the clutch.

Note that hand cranks turn slowly, usually less than 1 rpm, but have decent torque. Three [gearboxes](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Wiki/Guides/Gearbox) set to 3:1 with the arrows facing towards the handcrank(s) and a small generator are an effective way to recharge a small battery enough to start an engine within a few minutes.

### Auxiliary power units (APUs)

See [auxiliary power unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auxiliary_power_unit) at Wikipedia.

Many real-life aircraft carry an engine and generator solely dedicated to providing power for the aircraft. As the name suggests, this is a dedicated backup system. Generators connected to the main engines provide all power under normal circumstances, although the APU may be used to initially power up the aircraft before takeoff if ground power is unavailable. Further, in the event of simultaneous engine failure, the APU can be switched on in-flight to maintain power to control surfaces, fuel pumps, landing gear hydraulics, de-icing systems, and life support to buy time for the engine failure to be diagnosed and corrected, or, if all else fails, to at least facilitate an attempted [deadstick landing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deadstick_landing).

For Stormworks, much of the same logic applies. If an aircraft has just one battery at the bottom of the hull and it gets hit by a single round of ammo from a rotary autocannon, the engines will likely shut down in most designs, because:

- If a throttle is used to control engine throttle, an unpowered throttle will suddenly output 0, resulting in engine shutdown.

- If a clutch is used, an unpowered clutch will stop working resulting in total loss of power transmission from the engine to the rotor / propellers.

In addition to likely loss of engine power, all control surfaces will shut down, landing gears will be inoperable, pumps for fire suppression systems will not run, and mounted welders will be unable to repair the situation. With a backup battery, electric relay, backup generator, and appropriate microcontroller, the aircraft could automatically get power back on, extinguish the fire(s), and repair the main battery along with any other critical systems protected by mounted welders.

Note that a basic APU can be made with a small diesel engine, a gearbox set at 3:2 (arrows facing the engine), and a medium generator. The generator will produce 36 swatts while the engine will run at 8.16 rps and consume 0.06L of diesel per second. The power is a bit more than enough to run one mounted welder at a time.

title: Survivor
text:
# Survivor

| [![Stub](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/stormworks_gamepedia_en/images/f/f1/Stub_v1.png/revision/latest/scale-to-width-down/64?cb=20250514003444)](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/stormworks_gamepedia_en/images/f/f1/Stub_v1.png/revision/latest?cb=20250514003444) | *This article is a [stub](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Category:Stubs). *You can help Us by [expanding it](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Survivor?action=edit). |
| --- | --- |

Survivors are NPCs in [missions](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Wiki/Missions) who need to be stabilized and transported to hospitals or [hospital ships](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Hospital_ship) to be rescued. Survivors carry [strobe lights](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Equipment#Small_Equipment) set with man-overboard-mode to automatically activate if they end up in the water. Rescuing a survivor rewards the player with $3,000 multiplied by their health (from 0 to 1), so bringing a half-healed survivor to a hospital will only reward $1,500. In [classic mode](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Gameplay/Gamemodes/Classic), the player also receives a [research](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Research) point for each rescued survivor, regardless of their health.

Survivors may be found incapacitated and require a defibrillator to resuscitate. Wounded survivors may also lose health over time, and can become incapacitated if they aren't periodically treated with a med kit or kept in a medical bed.

Survivors can be told to follow the player and will do so reasonably quickly, following along the exact route the player took. They can even follow by swimming over water and walking over rough terrain, although they can sometimes fail to follow the player if the player jumps. The player is also able to pick up and carry survivors which can be useful in any situations where they fail to follow the player.

title: Hospital ship
text:
# Hospital ship

Section: Landing

| [![Stub](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/stormworks_gamepedia_en/images/f/f1/Stub_v1.png/revision/latest/scale-to-width-down/64?cb=20250514003444)](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/stormworks_gamepedia_en/images/f/f1/Stub_v1.png/revision/latest?cb=20250514003444) | *This article is a [stub](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Category:Stubs). *You can help Us by [expanding it](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Hospital_ship?action=edit). |
| --- | --- |

Hospital ships are mobile hospitals where [survivors](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Survivor) can be dropped off. They slowly patrol long ocean routes, stopping for about 10 seconds at a time after about every 1-1.5 km, as well as very infrequent stops (around once every half hour or so) of several minutes.

The back of the ship has a helipad suitable for landing a small [helicopter](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Wiki/Guides/Helicopters), and there are [ladders](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Ladder) at the sides of the helipad going down to the water so players can climb up from a small boat. Rope anchors on both sides of the ladders are present to allow a small [boat](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Wiki/Vehicles/Water/Boat) to be tethered to the ship, allowing a player to transfer survivors to the ship and return to their boat while both are in motion.

The ship has a med bay just in front of the helipad, with two doors leading into it. These are the only unlocked doors on the ship. Survivors who have been brought into the med bay will count as 'rescued'.

## Tethering

To tether a boat to a hospital ship, you'll need a [rope](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Rope) and a rope anchor. To be able to use the ship's ladders, the rope anchor should be positioned close to the center of your boat (or at least not too close to the front) so that you'll have an area of your boat where you are safe to stand next to the ship's ladder. If you use a rope anchor at the very front of your boat, your boat will be behind the ladder, so you'd have to jump and catch the ladder which is very likely to fail. If you fail to catch the ladder, you'll fall into the water, get dragged underneath and between the ship and your own boat and left stranded assuming you manage to avoid being killed by a propeller. Depending on how rough the weather is, you may or may not be able to swim fast enough to catch up and try again. So, don't place the rope anchor all the way at the front.

When you are ready to tether to the hospital ship, carefully adjust your throttle to very slightly exceed the ship's speed and angle your boat to slowly drift into it from the side. As you come up to the rope anchor, set your rope length to 2 meters and then quickly tether the ship and your boat together. Once tethered, you can cut your throttle to save fuel, trip your circuit breaker to save power, and then transfer all of your rescued survivors up to the ship's deck and into the med bay.

## Landing

## Landing

Landing on the helipad with a small helicopter is not overly difficult as the helipad is fairly large and the ship remains remarkably stable even in rough weather. However, care must be taken when landing as the ship can stop unexpectedly.

For securing a helicopter to the pad (e.g. in case a tsunami is approaching), note that there are [small winches](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Small_winch) on both sides and one at the back. All the winches have ropes stowed next to them. This allows a player to attach the rope between the winch and a rope anchor on their helicopter, then winch it in to secure it. Be careful when removing the ropes - if you've winched the helicopter in tightly on all three winches and then suddenly detach one of the ropes, it can be yanked forcefully. Start by winching out a bit on all of the winches, then detach the ropes.

Trailers can be found at various industrial locations and freight terminals in Stormworks, and can be transported to other locations for varying amounts of money.

A blank built-in trailer is available in the presets.

## Design

Built-in trailers follow the same standard configuration as described below.

### Size

Trailers are 11 blocks wide x 17 blocks tall x 47 blocks long (2.75x4.25x11.75 m).

### Wheels

There are two pairs of double 5x5 wheels on both sides of the back of each trailer, for a total of eight wheels.

### Connectors

Trailers have an electric connector along the midline of the bottom surface near the front, 5 blocks away from being at the front edge. It is 5 blocks above ground level.

### Outriggers

There are two outriggers with robotic pivots to keep the trailer level when it is not being towed. These automatically pivot out of the way when the electric connector is connected.

### Logic

The trailer can be controlled through its electric connector. Numeric channel 1 controls the brakes. As for the boolean channels:

1. Left turn signal
2. Right turn signal
3. Brake lights
4. Reverse lights
5. Marker lights

title: Nuclear power
text:
# Nuclear power

Section: Reactor > Coolant

Nuclear power provides a way to generate large amounts of power at effectively zero cost. Due to reactors and associated steam power plants usually being quite large and heavy, it is typically used to power ships, although compact nuclear power plants can also power large ground vehicles like trains and even aircraft.

## Reactor

Reactors provide a heat source for [boilers](https://stormworks.fandom.com/wiki/Steam_boiler) to convert freshwater into steam. Reactors are built with nuclear fuel assemblies, control rods, and nuclear fuel rods. A chain reaction takes effect when multiple nuclear fuel assemblies loaded with nuclear fuel rods are adjacent to each other, and this rapidly produces heat. The heat can easily be excessive, so control rods adjacent to the fuel assemblies are required to dampen the reaction and prevent meltdown.

To begin reacting, nuclear fuel rods must be inserted into nuclear fuel assemblies. The rounded tip on the fuel rod is the end which must be inserted into the assembly. A mechanism to physically move the fuel rod into the assembly must be built, or you can use gravity, though this risks having the rods get stuck from time to time.

Even just a sliding connector track in the reactor and a sliding connector gripper on the fuel rods is enough to prevent the fuel rods from getting stuck, though many other approaches are equally effective. Note that if you want to get the fuel rods out of the assembly (e.g. in the event of a coolant leak causing overheating fuel rods), you cannot stop the reaction merely by releasing the rods from the fuel assemblies (using the fuel assembly logic node). That's the first step, but it will simply unlock the fuel rods. They then have to be physically moved out of position (ejected from the core) using some other mechanism, e.g. a sliding track or a piston.

Note that adjacent assemblies have a synergistic effect, so reactors with many adjacent fuel assemblies can become excessively hot. The desired operating temperature is generally on the low end of the range between 120-300 °C since 120 °C is hot enough to get a boiler producing at least a small amount of steam while 300 °C is hot enough to get a boiler producing steam so quickly that it is no longer feasible to pump water into it fast enough to keep it working properly. Note that any excess heat just means the fuel rods will be expended more quickly, so the best approach is to minimize the reactor temperature to whatever is required to keep the boiler's steam pressure up.

In contrast to the fuel assemblies, control rods are used to dampen the reaction. Control rods are placed adjacent to fuel assemblies and must be placed three blocks higher than the level at which the assembly was placed or else they will do nothing. Control rods have an adjustable 'insertion' value from 0 to 1 controlled by a numeric input, and can be inserted more to decrease reaction rate and thus reduce the temperature of adjacent fuel assemblies.

### Coolant

title: Nuclear power
text:
# Nuclear power

Section: Troubleshooting > Reactor not heating up

ed or else they will do nothing. Control rods have an adjustable 'insertion' value from 0 to 1 controlled by a numeric input, and can be inserted more to decrease reaction rate and thus reduce the temperature of adjacent fuel assemblies.

### Coolant

Reactors should have freshwater as coolant. Without water as a radiation moderator, fuel rods can easily overheat, spew out excessive radiation, and potentially melt down. It is often a good idea to set a fluid meter inside of a reactor and an alarm in case the fluid level drops below normal (e.g. due to damage). This may require ejecting the fuel rods until the reactor can be repaired and refilled.

A reactor filled with coolant will tend to have all fuel assemblies at the same temperature. As coolant level drops, the fuel assemblies closer to the center of the reactor will heat up more than the ones at the edges. This can result in some of the fuel assemblies reaching meltdown temperatures even while other assemblies appear to be working normally.

### Radiation

If a radiation detector picks up more than about 1.5, it's enough to cause radiation damage to nearby players within a few seconds. This is worth sounding an alarm (and possibly switching to a different reactor design). This is also generally a sign that a reactor is overheating and/or has lost its coolant water, so an emergency core ejection is usually required to prevent a meltdown.

Radiation has a cumulative effect on players, so the longer the player is near an intense source of radiation, the longer it will take to get rid of the radiation effect. Hazmat suits can be used to reduce radiation exposure. Radiation causes damage over time, so players exposed to large doses of it may need a medical bed and many med kits to survive.

### Meltdown

At over 1500 degrees, reactors will suffer a meltdown. This creates a large, invisible area of extremely hazardous radiation which will remain even after the vehicle which created it is gone. The radiation gradually decreases over time.

## Reactor configuration

Reactors have to balance size and weight with startup speed and longevity. Lightweight (e.g. aviation-grade) reactors tend to use a minimum number of fuel assemblies and control rods which leads to a slow startup and reduced maximum operating time. Many different reactor configurations are possible.

In the sections below, fuel assemblies are denoted with an 'F' and control rods are denoted with a 'C'.

### 4 assemblies

This is the smallest functional reactor configuration:

```
CC
FF
FF
CC
```

### 9 assemblies

```
 C C
CFFFC
CFFFC
CFFFC
 C C
```

At 0.45 control rod insertion, this reactor will hold a temperature of about 339 degrees.

## Troubleshooting

### Reactor overheating

Likely causes:

- No coolant / inadequate coolant. It is best practice to keep reactors filled with fresh water.

- Control rods not built exactly three blocks above the level that the fuel assemblies were placed on.

- Not enough control rods / too many fuel assemblies.

- Control rods insufficiently inserted. Try setting their insertion to 1 and see if the reactor cools down.

### Reactor not heating up

Likely causes:

- Not enough control rods / too many fuel assemblies.

- Control rods insufficiently inserted. Try setting their insertion to 1 and see if the reactor cools down.

### Reactor not heating up

Likely causes:

- Fuel rods not actually inserted (temperature reading from fuel assembly will be 0). Put the fuel rods on a sliding connector track with track grippers to make sure they slide into place correctly.

## Dimensions

Players can fit through spaces that are no smaller than two blocks wide (0.5 m). Walking upright requires a ceiling at least 7 blocks tall (1.75 m). Crouching is possible with a space at least 3 blocks tall (0.75 m).

## Speed

- Walking: 2.6 m/s
- Swimming: 4.5 m/s
- Crouching: 4.7 m/s
- Fast swimming: 4.7 m/s
- Sprinting: 7.5 m/s
- Sprinting+jumping ("bunnyhopping"): 9.0 m/s.

## Slopes

A player can walk up a slope of up to 45 degrees. A slope of 63 degrees (e.g. made with 2:1 blocks going steeply upward) will cause a player to slide down when not moving, but isn't particularly difficult to climb with a combination of forward sprinting and jumping. A slope of 76 degrees (e.g. made with 4:1 blocks going steeply upward) is very difficult to climb but can be achieved with repeated mashing of the jump key.

## Jumping

A player can jump up a height of 5 blocks (1.25 meters). If sprinting, jumping, and then crouching in mid-air, the player can jump up 6 blocks (1.5 meters).

## Falling

A player will take damage if falling onto a hard surface more than 7 meters below them. Damage increases with falls from greater heights.
